Gratitude is positively associated with health and well-being. Past studies of gratitude have primarily focused on the distinct cultural context of European Americans. The current studies aimed to extend gratitude research to Latino and East Asian Americans, 2 collectivistic contexts known to differently value positive emotions. Two studies explored whether Latino and East Asian Americans varied in gratitude experience and whether the disposition toward gratitude was associated with well-being for both. In Study 1, participants completed measures of the emotional experience and expression of gratitude. Latino Americans rated the desirability, appropriateness, frequency, and intensity of their gratitude experience–expression higher than did East Asian Americans. Moreover, European Americans' gratitude experience and expression was similar to those of Latino Americans and higher than those of East Asian Americans. In Study 2, participants completed measures of gratitude disposition and indicators of well-being. Latino Americans reported a higher disposition toward gratitude than did East Asian Americans. Higher disposition toward gratitude was associated with higher self-esteem and with less loneliness and perceived stress across groups. However, the strength of the association of gratitude with subjective health and depressive symptoms varied by group in theoretically expected ways. The promising possibilities of extending research on gratitude to culturally diverse groups is discussed.

Gratitude, as both a positive emotion and disposition, has been defined as the "generalized tendency to recognize and respond with grateful emotion to the roles of other people's benevolence in the positive experiences and outcomes that one obtains" (McCullough, Emmons, & Tsang, 2002 p. 112). search has linked gratitude to indicators of well-being and health, including lower levels of depression, anxiety, and negative affect (Hill, Allemand, & Roberts, 2013; Wood, Froh, & Geraghty, 2010). Studies have also found that individuals with a higher disposition toward gratitude tend to report higher life satisfaction, optimism, and positive affect and lower envy compared to individuals with a lower disposition toward gratitude (McCullough et al., 2002). A recent meta-analysis concluded that gratitude interventions are linked to positive outcomes, including happiness, well-being, and life satisfaction (Dickens, 2017). Little of this research, however, has studied gratitude in ethnically diverse samples.

Gratitude research to date has primarily studied U.S. college samples comprised of participants of mostly European American background (McCullough et al., 2002; Wood, Maltby, Stewart, Linley, & Joseph, 2008). However, a substantial empirical literature has documented cultural variations in emotional experiences and psychological outcomes that are relevant to gratitude. For example, Miller and Bersoff's (1992) work on reciprocity, a construct that is conceptually related to gratitude, suggests that cul-

tural context plays a role in the norms and motivations of helping behaviors. Their studies showed that European Americans were more likely to classify helping as a social obligation when it was part of a reciprocal exchange compared to when helping occurred spontaneously. In contrast, Hindu Indians viewed helping as reflecting intrinsic motivations regardless of expectations for reciprocal exchange (Miller & Bersoff, 1992). Moreover, experiences of engaging emotions (e.g., feelings of respect) were found to predict general positive feelings among Japanese participants, whereas the experience of disengaging emotions (i.e., pride) predicted general happiness among Americans (Kitayama, Mesquita, & Karasawa, 2006). Gratitude can be considered an engaging emotion because it encourages connectedness and fosters harmonious relationships. These cultural variations may have implications for gratitude, which is commonly evoked by the perception that one has benefited from another's help and is considered important for social exchanges and relationships (Algoe, Haidt, &

Culture plays a central role in emotional experiences that implicate the self as well as relationships to others (Markus & Kitayama, 1991). Individuals with interdependent selves are more likely to experience and express other-focused emotions (e.g., sympathy) compared to persons with independent selves (Markus & Kitayama, 1991). Although Latinos and East Asians share norms of cultural interdependence, they differ regarding the expression of positive emotion. Latino culture places value on open expression of positive emotions, whereas East Asian cultures place value on suppressing emotions, including positive emotions, in order to maintain interpersonal harmony (Ruby, Falk, Heine, Villa, & Silberstein, 2012). For example, Ruby and colleagues (2012) also showed that individuals of Latino background place a greater value on high-activation positive emotions (e.g., excited, enthusiastic, and elated vs. calm, at rest, and serene) than do East Asians.

We hypothesized that the experience and expression of gratitude would be more strongly valued by Latinos than East Asians (Study 1). We also compared our Latino and East Asian samples with an independent culture (e.g., European Americans) to better situate our findings within the existing literature. We then explored the associations between disposition toward gratitude and well-being among Latinos and East Asians in Study 2. Data sets are publicly available at http://doi.org/10.3886/E103420V1 (Corona, 2018).

Participants. Latino (n = 666; 18.2% men), East Asian (n = 464; 26.3% men), and European (n = 491; 30.5% men) American university students were recruited as part of a larger study. The majority of Latino participants were of Mexican heritage (n = 537), with 87 reporting another Latino ethnicity (e.g., Guatemalan) and 42 reporting a combination of Latino ethnicities. East Asians were Chinese (n = 325), Korean (n = 111), Japanese (n = 18), or a combination of these (n = 10). The sample ranged in age from 18 to 54 (n = 10). The sample ranged in age from 18 to 54 (n = 10), SD = 2.65). Institutional Review Board approval was obtained from Georgetown University; University of California, Irvine; and Arizona State University.

Measures. Eight items adapted from Eid and Diener (2001) measured dimensions of the experience and expression of gratitude (information on adapted measures is included in the online supplemental materials). In four items, participants were asked to indicate how desirable and appropriate it is to experience and express a list of emotions, including gratitude. Items were rated on a 7-point scale from 1 (Extremely undesirable/inappropriate) to 7 (Extremely desirable/appropriate). Participants were also asked to choose a number reflecting the number of times during the past week they had felt and expressed each emotion. These items were rated on a 7-point scale from 1 (0-1 times) to 7 (At least once per day). Finally, to establish a common reference point across cultural groups, we asked participants in each group to rate the intensity of their gratitude experience and expression relative to that of a typical European American. These items were rated on a 7-point scale from 1 (None, I never experience it/express it) to 7 (Extremely Intense). Information on sample-size determination, dataexclusion decisions, manipulations, and all measures for both studies are included in the online supplemental materials.

We used eight separate one-way analyses of variance with Tukey post hoc tests to examine mean differences in each gratitude item (see Table 1 and also the online supplemental materials). Power analysis using g*Power revealed that given our group sizes, we had a 90% chance of detecting a small effect as significant at

the 5% level. As expected, Latinos reported significantly higher desirability of experiencing and expressing gratitude than did East Asians. Latinos also rated the appropriateness of expressing gratitude, the frequency of its expression, and the intensity of experience and expression higher than did East Asians. However, Latinos did not report experiencing gratitude more frequently than did East Asians.

Consistent with broader literature on cultural variation in emotion, results indicated that Asian Americans' desirability of experience and expression were significantly lower than were Latinos' and European Americans'. European Americans rated the appropriateness of experiencing and expressing gratitude higher than did both groups. European Americans also reported experiencing gratitude more frequently than did both groups and expressing gratitude more frequently than did East Asians. Last, European Americans reported greater intensity of experience and expression than did East Asians.

The observed variation in desirability and appropriateness ratings was consistent with research showing that positive emotions are differentially valued across Latino and Asian collectivist culture contexts (Ruby et al., 2012); they also differed in theoretically expected ways from those of the European American sample. To further understand gratitude differences in the two target groups, Study 2 explored the association of gratitude with subjective health, depressive symptoms, self-esteem, loneliness, and perceived stress in Latinos and East Asians. Study 2 also explored whether observed effects would be unique to gratitude or a reflection of broader cultural differences in positive affect. Fully examining that possibility will be a topic of future research, but we sought to address it in Study 2 by assessing whether observed effects of gratitude persist after the variance contributed by positive affect was accounted for in our model.

Participants. Latino (n=91; 13.2% men) and East Asian (n=121; 15.7% men) university students were selected from a larger study (N=287). Participants were recruited through the university's human subject pool. Sixty-seven participants were of Mexican–Mexican American background, and 24 participants were from South–Central American backgrounds. Sixty of the East Asian participants reported Chinese background, three reported a Japanese background, 21 reported a Korean background, and 37 were of mixed East Asian backgrounds. The sample ranged in age from 18 to 43 (M=20.89, SD=3.07). Study procedures were approved by the University of California, Irvine, Institutional Review Board.

Measures. The Gratitude Questionnaire—Six-Item Form measured individuals' tendency to experience gratitude in daily life (i.e., intensity, frequency, span, and density) on a 7-point scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree; McCullough et al., 2002). Cronbach's alpha for gratitude was .84 for both Latino and East Asian Americans. Subjective health was assessed using two items: "How would you characterize your health?" and "Your health is _ compared with others your age (and gender)?" on a 5-point Likert-type scale from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent; Quesnel-Vallée, 2007). Cronbach's alpha was .87 for Latinos and .93 for

East Asians. Self-esteem was measured using the Single-Item Self-Esteem Scale on a 5-point scale from 1 (strongly agree) to 5 (strongly disagree; Robins, Hendin, & Trzesniewski, 2001). The 20-item UCLA Loneliness Scale measured subjective feelings of social isolation (Russell, Peplau, & Ferguson, 1978). Ratings were on a 4-point scale from 1 (always) to 4 (never). The Cronbach's alpha was .94 for both groups. The 14-item Perceived Stress Scale measured the degree to which the demands participants experienced exceeded their ability to cope on a 5-point scale from 1 (never) to 5 (almost always; Cohen, Kamarck, & Mermelstein, 1983). Cronbach's alpha was .85 for Latinos and .89 for East Asians. The nine-item Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale asked how often participants experienced depressive symptoms in the past 7 days, rated on a 4-point Likert-type scale from 1 (rarely or none of the time) to 4 (most or all of the time; Santor & Coyne, 1997). Cronbach's alpha was .91 for Latinos and .93 for East Asians. The 20-item Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (Watson, Clark, & Tellegen, 1988) measured how participants felt in general by rating the intensity of positive and negative emotions on a 5-point scale from 1 (very slightly or not at all) to 5 (extremely). In the present study, only positive affect was included in the analyses to test for the unique effect of gratitude. Cronbach's alpha was .89 for Latinos and .90 for East Asians.

Bivariate correlations are presented in Table 2. Means, standard deviations, and t test values are presented in Table 3 (see also the online supplemental materials). To meet the assumptions of normality, gratitude was square-root-transformed and reflected, whereas depressive symptoms were square-root-transformed. We conducted regression analyses to assess the relationship between disposition toward gratitude and well-being. Model 1 included gender as a covariate because previous work has found that men and women derive different benefits from gratitude, such as greater relatedness, but our small sample of men precluded testing for possible gender variation (Kashdan, Mishra, Breen, & Froh, 2009). Model 2 included an ethnic background variable that was dummycoded using East Asians as the reference group and the disposition toward gratitude variable. Model 3 included a two-way interaction between gratitude and ethnic background. All variables were centered per Aiken and West (1991). Model 4 included positive affect to test whether observed effects were unique to gratitude or broadly reflective of positive emotions.

As in Study 1, Latinos (M = -2.50, SD = 1.07)^2 reported higher gratitude levels than did East Asians (M = -2.80, SD = 1.04). A post hoc power analysis revealed that the power to obtain the detected effects at the .05 level was .53. In Table 4, the row showing the interaction effect for gratitude across Model 3 shows there was a significant interaction between ethnicity and disposition toward gratitude for two out of five outcome variables. cating that the gratitude effect was greater in East Asians than in Latinos (see Table 4). We interpret these interactions as suggesting that some benefits to health and well-being that arise from having a high disposition toward gratitude may vary by ethnic background. The row showing the main effect for gratitude across Model 2 shows a greater disposition toward gratitude was also associated with less loneliness, less perceived stress, and higher self-esteem for both groups. Last, the group differences in the effects of gratitude remained after controlling for positive affect, suggesting that the observed gratitude differences are unique to this positive emotion.

This research is the first to study gratitude and its associations with well-being in Latinos and East Asians. Relative to East Asians, Latinos reported experiencing gratitude more frequently and intensely (Study 1 and Study 2), expressing gratitude more frequently and intensely (Study 2), and believing gratitude was more appropriate and desirable (Study 1). These differences are consistent with an emerging literature on differences within interdependent groups (Boiger, Güngör, Karasawa, & Mesquita, 2014; Ruby et al., 2012). Our work indicated that gratitude experience and expression may be more similar among European Americans and Latinos than among European Americans and East Asians. The main contribution of this work is demonstrating that these two collectivist groups differ on one important positive emotion, grat-

itude. These intriguing findings on cultural variation are preliminary, but given that gratitude is important for relationships and adaptive for health, they signal an important direction for future research.

These studies also showed that gratitude was negatively associated with loneliness, perceived stress, and depression and positively associated with self-esteem and subjective health. This work is consistent with McCullough et al. (2002) showing that gratitude is related to positive affect and negative affect, including anxiety and depression. Overall, gratitude was moderately to strongly associated with well-being in both Latinos and East Asians; however, the associations of gratitude with subjective health and depressive symptoms were stronger for East Asians. Because Latinos rated their gratitude higher than did East Asians, these variations cannot be explained by the differences found in gratitude across the groups. Rather, it may be that in East Asians, gratitude levels were consistent with cultural values and norms and thus associated with well-being benefits even though gratitude was not expressed or experienced at high levels as much as in comparison groups. Also, the difference found in gratitude effects across groups cannot be explained by positive affect.

Our results indicate that researchers should be cautious about assuming that the experience and expression of gratitude is highly desirable across groups. Future research should also focus on whether these cultural variations generalize to other positive emotions as well as possible mechanisms that help explain the con-

nection between well-being and gratitude disposition across cultural contexts. One possibility is that the extent to which gratitude covaries with feelings of obligation is particularly relevant in collectivist contexts. Perhaps individuals with a strong sense of obligation to their close others may feel more gratitude and, in turn, experience positive outcomes. It should also be noted that measures of well-being often actually address "ill-being" (e.g., depressive symptoms). Although this is a common problem in the literature, it still allows an examination of ethnic variation in the associations of gratitude with relevant indicators of well-being.

We acknowledge that these studies are limited in their generalizability. The samples were composed of undergraduates, and therefore the generalizability is limited by the sample's age range and socioeconomic status. The conclusions are also constrained to interdependent samples for whom U.S. culture may influence the experience and expression of emotions. On the other hand, although interdependence may be attenuated in U.S. groups with heritages from interdependent societies, there is still extensive evidence suggesting that Latinos and Asians in the United States retain cultural interdependence. It is also possible that gratitude experiences and expressions are different in places where interdependent individuals are the majority and collectivist norms prevail. Evidence has suggested that ethnic minorities retain emotional tendencies from heritage cultures (e.g., Tsai & Chentsova-Dutton, 2003), but it is optimal for future studies to be run in less Americanized samples (e.g., Mexico, China). Future studies should also focus on psychometrics to better understand gratitude and variation in gratitude across cultural groups. In our studies, we sought evidence of overall cultural differences in response bias as a way to better understand whether our ethnic group samples differed in how they approached the gratitude measure. We tested for the significance of difference in variances in Study 2 well-being measures, which were distributed around the midpoints of the scales, and did not find any. Nonetheless, future research on this topic needs to establish more clearly whether restriction of range is a problem through confirmatory factor analyses. A more diverse database may also help in understanding whether specific sociocultural variables facilitate and/or promote feelings of gratitude.

We hope this exploration inspires more research on gratitude experience across ethnic and cultural groups. The findings raise important questions. For example, how is gratitude interpreted and defined differently across ethnicities? What role does gratitude play in social relationship building and solidifying relationships among diverse groups? Over time, this may yield a more inclusive research literature and a greater understanding of the conditions that set the stage for deriving maximum benefits from gratitude.
